subject: Estimate a model with a long vector of latent discrete parameters in Stan

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Estimate a model with a long vector of latent discrete parameters in Stan
parts:
Hi,

I am estimating a model for animal movement where in each time step the animal is in one of two Z states:

- '0' state - foraging: the animal searches for food; moving relatively short distances per time step.
- '1' state - Migrating: the animal is moving to a far-away destination, and hence moves long distances per time step.

I attach fake data for this problem (the true state of the animal is in the 'Z' part of the list, and the distance moved is in the 'l' part of the list). Visually it is fairly obvious as to which state the animal is in at any point in time. I would like to use Stan to try to estimate the state of the animal at a given time step, given its distance moved in this step and all past steps. 

I am generating the fake data by assuming that the state is persistent; an animal remains foraging or migrating for multiple time steps. I want to estimate a model in Stan that similarly allows for a persistence in State.

The issue here is that the state is discrete, and more troubling, it takes on a value for each of the time periods (I have chosen N=200 for the fake data I attach, although the real data is around 10000 time steps.) The issue with this long data is that I can't see a way to marginalise out the latent variable. Instead at the moment I have tried to use a continuous latent variable, constrained between 0 and 1, with a switch at 0.5 that dictates the actual state of the system for each time point. The code for this model is below.

Unsurprisingly this model doesn't work. The chains for the 'Z_continuous' parameters aren't mixing at all; I suppose this is because the log-probability does not vary with this variable unless it crosses 0.5.

Does anyone have an idea as to how I might be able to estimate this model, or a similarly-behaving one in Stan?

Further information: I have estimated the model in JAGS, and it works well; the model is very good at returning the state 'Z' at any point in time. The issue however is speed; JAGS is slow, and as such will be impossible to use to estimate the full data set. If I can't get this to work in Stan then I may try 'pymc3', although have never used it before. It also occurs to me that I could do some sort of particle MC sampling here. However, any other ideas are also very welcome!

Best,

Ben

data {
  int N; ## Num obs
  real<lower=0> l[N]; ## Distance moved
  real<lower=0> aPrior0;
  real<lower=0> aPriorExtra;
}

parameters{
  real<lower=0,upper=1> Z_continuous[N];
  real<lower=0> a0;
  real<lower=0> aExtra;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

transformed parameters{
  real Z[N];
  for(t in 1:N){
    Z[t] = Z_continuous[t] > 0.5;
  }
}

model{
  for(t in 2:N){
    if(Z_continuous[t]<0.5){
      l[t] ~ exponential(a0+aExtra);
    } else{
      l[t] ~ exponential(a0);
    }
    Z_continuous[t] ~ normal(Z_continuous[t-1],sigma);
  }
  a0 ~ exponential(aPrior0);
  aExtra ~ exponential(aPriorExtra);
}

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimate a model with a long vector of latent discrete parameters in Stan
parts: Have you considered a mixture model over the two states? Something along the lines of:

data {
  int N; ## Num obs
  real<lower=0> l[N]; ## Distance moved
  real<lower=0> aPrior0;
  real<lower=0> aPriorExtra;
}

parameters{
real state_logit[N]; //mixture probs on logit scale

real<lower=0> a0;
  real<lower=0> aExtra;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model{

a0 ~ exponential(aPrior0);
  aExtra ~ exponential(aPriorExtra);

state_logit[1] ~ normal(0,sigma); // you seemed to forget this, so I'm guessing at what you might want as the prior here
  for(t in 2:N){
    state_logit[t] ~ normal(state_logit[t-1],sigma);
    target += log_sum_exp(
        log(inv_logit(state_logit[t])) + exponential_lpdf( l | a0 + aExtra )
        , log1m(inv_logit(state_logit[t])) + exponential_lpdf( l | a0 )
    ) ;
  }

}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimate a model with a long vector of latent discrete parameters in Stan
parts:
Good timing. I was at ISEC watching all the movement
HMM talks and decided to code it with simulated data
myself. It's just an HMM, so it's dead easy to marginalize.

I followed the conventions on change-in-bearing
being in (-pi, pi) of the moveHMM R package (on CRAN).

data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N] turn;
vector<lower=0>[N] dist;
int<lower=1> K;
}
parameters {
simplex[K] theta[K];
vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[K] mu;
vector<lower=0>[K] kappa;
positive_ordered[K] alpha;
vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
}
model {
vector[K] log_theta[K];
vector[K] lp;

for (k in 1:K) log_theta[k] = log(theta[k]);
lp = rep_vector(-log(K), K);
for (n in 1:N) {
for (k in 1:K)
lp[k]
= log_sum_exp(log_theta[k] + lp)
+ von_mises_lpdf(turn[n] | mu[k], kappa[k])
+ lognormal_lpdf(dist[n] | alpha[k], sigma[k]);
}
target += log_sum_exp(lp);

kappa ~ lognormal(0, 2);
alpha ~ lognormal(0, 2);
sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);
}

It uses the new Stan 2.10 model notation.

lp stores a column of values in the forward-backward algorithm
on the log scale.

see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward–backward_algorithm

You can see that through this relation (a is the transition
matrix and b is the current log densities of ending in
the particular state given the input data):

log(a' * b) = log(sum(a .* b))

= log(sum(a[1] * b[1] + ... + a[N] * b[N]))

= log(sum(exp(log(a[1] * b[1]) + ... + exp(log(a[N] * b[N])))))

= log(sum(exp(log(a[1]) + log(b[1])) + ...)

= log_sum_exp(log(a[1]) + log(b[1]), ..., log(a[N]) + log(b[N]))

= log_sum_exp(log(a) + log(b))

At the end, I only need to log_sum_exp the final forward state to
get the final likelihood for (turn[n], dist[n]) (so it's not a bug
that the target += is inot in the loop).

I didn't think too hard about priors. It does a reasonable,
but not great, job of recovering simulated parameters. And you
can swap in Weibull or whatever makes sense for the step sizes.
I just used a von Mises on the change in bearing---our von Mises
lets you choose your own interval.

And you can easily turn the transitions into multi-logit regressions.

I ran the simulation for N = 10,000 and it worked fine and ran in
about 6 minutes on my Mac notebook (using RStan 2.10) and got
a reasonable n_eff using a single chain for 200 iterations:

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
theta[1,1] 0.91 0.00 0.00 0.90 0.91 0.91 0.92 0.92 30 1.00
theta[1,2] 0.09 0.00 0.00 0.08 0.08 0.09 0.09 0.10 30 1.00
theta[2,1] 0.07 0.00 0.00 0.06 0.07 0.07 0.07 0.07 61 1.01
theta[2,2] 0.93 0.00 0.00 0.93 0.93 0.93 0.93 0.94 61 1.01
mu[1] -0.21 0.01 0.05 -0.30 -0.24 -0.21 -0.18 -0.12 72 0.99
mu[2] -0.02 0.00 0.01 -0.03 -0.02 -0.02 -0.01 0.00 86 1.07
kappa[1] 0.49 0.00 0.02 0.43 0.47 0.49 0.50 0.52 50 1.00
kappa[2] 2.96 0.00 0.05 2.88 2.92 2.96 2.99 3.05 100 0.99
alpha[1] 1.00 0.00 0.00 1.00 1.00 1.00 1.01 1.01 100 0.99
alpha[2] 2.78 0.00 0.01 2.76 2.77 2.78 2.78 2.80 100 0.99
sigma[1] 0.25 0.00 0.00 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.26 100 0.99
sigma[2] 0.78 0.00 0.01 0.77 0.78 0.79 0.79 0.81 100 1.00

vs. simulated:

alpha_dist <- c(1, 3);
sigma_dist <- c(0.25, 0.5);

mu_turn <- c(-0.2, 0);
kappa_turn <- c(0.5, 4);

You'll probably want to think harder about priors and likelihood to
avoid the sampler or optimizer getting stuck in a mode (or at a likelihood
spike at a boundary). Also, this is just using
the precision-like value kappa (bigger is lower variance).

From examples I've run, it tends to overestimate
the time it stays in a state and overestimate the deviation
on the movement sizes, but I haven't done a controlled study.
I think this may be inherent to the kind of mixture modeling
being done here, with the bias coming from the 90% remain-in-state
probabilities making each state want to soak up boundary cases
it wouldn't otherwise soak up. But I'm not sure.

I'll attach the Stan file and the data simulator and the code to run it.
I made the simulated data easily separable just to make sure the algorithm
was coded properly.

I'm also attaching a file to read from the moveHMM sample data,
which also fits OK with the Weibull that they use (I didn't use
the covariates). I wanted to go through the logic of turning
angle to make sure I did it right.

I'll write this all up as a regular case study when I get the chance.

- Bob

parts:
Hi Bob,

That's great - thanks very much for this. The elk study (I'm sure you know) is very much the canonical paper on this topic, so very useful to see it.

Just trying to understand it and had a few questions:

1. The model you provide estimates the transition matrix for switching between the two states of the system across all time. Is there a way to estimate the state of the system at a given point in time? Essentially this would be a continuous variable of length N that represents the probability of being in one of two states.

2. Is this model extendable to allow a switching probability that depends on covariates?

Best,

Ben

parts:
> On Jul 5, 2016, at 8:46 AM, 'Ben Lambert' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

Is there a way to estimate the state of the system at a given point in time? Essentially this would be a continuous variable of length N that represents the probability of being in one of two states.

Yes, you just need the backward part of the forward-backward
algorithm. I can put that in the case study. It's just as
straightforward as the forward algorithm.
> 2. Is this model extendable to allow a switching probability that depends on covariates?

Yes, that's what I meant when I said you could also model the
transitions as a multi-logit. There are examples in the manual on
how to code these. I don't know if people use a one-hot state vector
as a predictor or just write K different regressions.

Either way, the forward algorithm will work for general state-space
models.

- Bob

Hi Bob,

The full code is below (I basically got the backwards part from the Stan manual, and - to be honest - I don't really understand it! Any clarification on how it works would be great.) Using it on fake data, it seems to do a pretty good job of returning the state vector. 

Also, I want to record the log-likelihood for each data point so I can calculate WAIC etc. Do you know how I can do this?

Best,

Ben

functions{
  ## Function that returns the log pdf of the wrapped-Cauchy
  real wrappedCauchy(real aPhi, real aRho, real aMu) {
    return(- log(2*pi()) + log((1-aRho^2)/(1+aRho^2-2*aRho*cos(aPhi-aMu))));
  }
  
  ## Function that returns a random sample from wrapped-Cauchy by first
  ## sampling from the Cauchy, then using modular arithmetic
  real wrappedCauchy_rng(real aRho, real aMu){
    real aCauchyRand;
    real aWCRand;
    
    aCauchyRand = cauchy_rng(pi()+aMu,-log(aRho));
    if (aCauchyRand>0){
      aWCRand = fmod(aCauchyRand,2*pi()) - pi();
    } else{
      aWCRand = -fmod(-aCauchyRand,2*pi()) + pi();   
    }

    return(aWCRand);
  }
  
}

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N] phi;
  vector<lower=0>[N] l;

int<lower=1> K;
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta[K];
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[K] mu;

real<lower=0,upper=1> rho[K];
  positive_ordered[K] alpha;
  positive_ordered[K] beta;

}  
model {
  vector[K] log_theta[K];
  vector[K] lp;

  for (k in 1:K) log_theta[k] = log(theta[k]);
lp = rep_vector(-log(K), K); ## Initial state log-probability

for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K){
      lp[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta[k] + lp)

+ wrappedCauchy(phi[n], rho[k], mu[k])
        + weibull_lpdf(l[n]| alpha[k], beta[k]);
    }
  }
  target += log_sum_exp(lp);

  alpha[1] ~ normal(5,5);
  alpha[2] ~ normal(20,5);
  beta[1] ~ normal(200,5);
  beta[2] ~ normal(1000,5);
  rho[1] ~ beta(2,10);
  rho[2] ~ beta(8,10);
  
}


generated quantities {
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y_star[N];
  real log_p_y_star;
  
  ## Do backwards algorithm to get the estimated states
  {
    int back_ptr[N, K];
    real best_logp[N, K];
    real best_total_logp;
for (k in 1:K)

best_logp[1, K] = wrappedCauchy(phi[1], rho[k], mu[k])
                      + weibull_lpdf(l[1] | alpha[k], beta[k]);
    for (t in 2:N) {
      for (k in 1:K) {
      best_logp[t, k] = negative_infinity();
        for (j in 1:K) {
          real logp;
          logp = best_logp[t-1, j]
          + log(theta[j, k]) + wrappedCauchy(phi[t], rho[k], mu[k])
                             + weibull_lpdf(l[t] | alpha[k], beta[k]);
          if (logp > best_logp[t, k]) {
            back_ptr[t, k] = j;
            best_logp[t, k] = logp;
          }
        }
      }
    }
    log_p_y_star = max(best_logp[N]);
for (k in 1:K)

if (best_logp[N, k] == log_p_y_star)
      y_star[N] = k;
      for (t in 1:(N - 1))
      y_star[N - t] = back_ptr[N - t + 1,
      y_star[N - t + 1]];
  }

}

Yes, the log likelihood is just the bit you're incrementing
target += with! The rest is the prior.

You should work through how the forward and backward algorithm
work if you're going to continue in this area. It's not that
hard and is a good exercise in marginalization!
